segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Good morning,everyone.In the last few lectures I've been dealing with businessfinance, but now I'm going to move on to businesssystems.And in today's lecture I'm going to talk about what can go wrong when businessestry to copy their own best practices.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Once a business has successfullyintroduceda new process- managinga branch bank, say, or selling a new product- the parent organisationnaturallywants to that success, and capture it if possibleon a bigger scale.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The goal, then, is to utilise existing knowledgeand not to generate new knowledge.It's a less glamorousactivity than pure I innovation,but it actually happensmore often, as a matter of fact.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: However,surprisingly, 031 getting things right the secondtime is not necessarilyany simpler than it was tile first time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Ii Now, there's been a lot of researchinto how companiescan their previous successes,and it ce1ainly hasn't been confinedto the United States.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It seems that most large industriesare trying to repeattheir own successes,and managethe knowledge they've acquired- but even so it has been shown that the overwhelmingmajorityof attemptsfail.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: A host of studies confirmthis, covering a wide range of businesssettings: 032 branch banks, retail stores, real estate agencies,factories, call centres ... to name but a few.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: So why do·so few managersget things right the second or third time?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Let's considerone reason for failure - placingtoo much trust in the peoplewho are runningthe successful operation,the 'experts' shall we say.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Managerswho want to apply existing knowledge typically start off by going to an expert - such as the personwho designedand is running a successfuldepartmentstore - and pickingtheir brains.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now, this approachcan be used if 033 II you,want to gain a rough understandingof a particularsystem,or understandsmaller, isolated problems.The trouble is, even the expert doesn't fully grasp the whole thing becausewhen it comes to complexsystems,the individualcomponentsof the process are interwovenwith one another.The expert never has completeaccess to the necessary information.And the situation'scomplicatedeven further by the fact that experts are usually not aware oftheir own ignorance.The ignorancecan take various forms.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For instance,a lot of details of the system are invisibleto managers.Some may be difficult to describe 034 learned on the job and well known by workers perhaps,but impossibleto describe in a way that's helpful.And there are some things that people know or do that they're not even aware of.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Now, let's considertwo types of mistakethat can occur when a manager actually starts to set up a duplicate systemto replicatea successfulprocess.Firstly, perhapshe forgets that he was just trying to copy anotherprocess,and starts trying to improveon it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Another mistake is trying to use the best parts of various different systems, in the hope of creating the perfect combination. 035 Unfortunately,attempts like these usuallyturn out to be misguidedand lead to problems.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Why?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Well, for various reasons.Perhapsthere weren't really any advantagesafter all, becausethe informationwasn't accurate.Or perhapsthe businesssettingsweren't really comparable.More typically,the advantagesare real enough, but there are also disadvantagesthat have been overlooked.For ,the modificationsmight compromisesafety in some way. 036 So, what's the solution?Well, I don't intend to suggestthat it's easy to get things right the second time ... it's not.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But the underlyingproblemhas more to do with attitudesthan the actual difficulty of the task, and there are ways of getting it right.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These involve adjusting attitudes,first of all ... being more realisticand cautious really.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Secondly,they involve 037 exerting strict controlson the organisationaland operationalsystems.And this in turn 038 means copyingthe original as closely as possible.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Not merely duplicatingthe physical characteristicsof the factory, but also duplicatingthe skills that the original employeeshad. & 40 Reliance on a template like this offers the huge advantageof built-in consistency. ••Iii•
